title: Global leading-symbol calculus for real pseudodifferential operators
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field]. Let $N$ be a compact oriented smooth manifold without boundary of dimension $m\geq1$, with a smooth Riemannian metric and its positive volume form $dV$. Let $E,F,G$ be smooth finite-rank real vector bundles. Use the distribution spaces, symbol classes $S^r$ and operator classes $\Psi^r$ of [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators]. Write $E_{\mathbf C}=E\otimes_{\mathbf R}\mathbf C$ and likewise for the other bundles. For $r\in\mathbf Z$, let $b(x,\xi):E_{\mathbf C,x}\to F_{\mathbf C,x}$ be smooth on $T^*N\setminus0$, positively homogeneous of degree $r$, and satisfy $b(x,-\xi)=\overline{b(x,\xi)}$ in real frames. Say that $T\in\Psi^r(E,F)$ has homogeneous leading symbol $b$ if, in every common coordinate trivialization and for all real $\chi,\psi\in C_c^\infty$ in that chart, $$\chi T\psi-\chi\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Op}(\theta b)\psi\in\Psi^{r-1}(E,F).$$ The chart operator in this formula is extended by zero after the cutoffs; $\theta(\xi)$ is any smooth real radial function zero for $|\xi|\leq1$ and one for $|\xi|\geq2$. Then the following hold. (i) For every such $b$ there exists a real $T\in\Psi^r(E,F)$ with leading symbol $b$. Two operators of order $r$ with the same leading symbol differ by an element of $\Psi^{r-1}(E,F)$. (ii) Each $\Psi^r(E,F)$ is a real vector space, $\Psi^{r-1}(E,F)\subseteq\Psi^r(E,F)$, and $$S\circ T\in\Psi^{s+r}(E,G)\quad(T\in\Psi^r(E,F),\ S\in\Psi^s(F,G)).$$ If $T,S$ have homogeneous leading symbols $b,c$, respectively, their composite has homogeneous leading symbol $cb$. (iii) The identity has order zero and leading symbol $\operatorname{id}$. A real smooth-coefficient differential operator $D:E\to F$ of order at most $k\geq0$, locally $D=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}a_\alpha(x)\partial^\alpha$, extended by the same differential expression to distributions, belongs to $\Psi^k(E,F)$ and has homogeneous leading symbol $$p_k(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=k}a_\alpha(x)(i\xi)^\alpha.$$ In particular this formula defines a global bundle symbol. All memberships, differences and composition statements concern the given maps on all distributions.

source.place: Demailly, Part I §3.B, printed pp.12–14 (PDF pages 24–26); WANTED locally, read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/hodge-ams.pdf; (3.4)–(3.5), global quantization before Proposition 3.6, and composition Proposition 3.7, printed pp.12–13; leading-symbol formulation and real conjugation symmetry made explicit.

proof.text: First establish the local calculus for the given maps on distributions. A localized quantization has amplitude $\chi(x)a(x,\xi)\psi(y)$; the amplitude-reduction theorem supplies its continuous transpose, its smooth off-diagonal kernel, and a left symbol with diagonal term $\chi\psi a$ modulo $S^{r-1}$. The coordinate-change theorem gives exactly the cotangent transformation and the frame factors in every other chart. Use real symbols throughout by replacing $a$ by $a_{\mathbf R}=(a(x,\xi)+\overline{a(x,-\xi)})/2$; amplitude reduction says this replacement equals the original real-part operator on every distribution. Both input and output cutoffs remain inside the transpose. No equality on a dense subspace is being substituted for equality on distributions.

proof.text: The order filtration and real-vector-space assertions follow directly by concatenating finite representations, multiplying their symbols by real scalars, and adding their smooth kernels: the symbol inequalities are stable under these operations, and $(1+|\xi|)^{r-1-|\beta|}\leq(1+|\xi|)^{r-|\beta|}$. We will also use localization: multiplying either side by a smooth scalar just replaces an amplitude by that scalar times the amplitude, so it preserves order by amplitude reduction. Smoothing terms cause no obstruction in compositions: for a local term $L$, the kernels of $LR_K$ and $R_KL$ are obtained by applying $L$ in $x$, respectively its bilinear density transpose in $y$, to the smooth kernel. They are smooth jointly: difference quotients of a smooth parameter family of tests converge in every smooth seminorm on the fixed compact support, and continuity of the test map commutes with these limits and all iterated derivatives. This applies entrywise to bundle kernels in a finite atlas; hence both composites are smooth-kernel operators. All these kernel formulas agree on distributions by transposition.

proof.text: Choose a finite cover by relatively compact coordinate domains trivializing the bundles. Apply the subordinate-partition theorem with $S=N$ to obtain real $\rho_i$ with $\sum_i\rho_i=1$ and compact support in $U_i$. Obtain $\eta_i\in C_c^\infty(U_i)$ equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i$ from smooth separation, using a relatively compact intermediate neighborhood. Compact manifolds here are Hausdorff, sigma-compact and normal. Set $a_i=\theta b_i$ in the chart and $T_b=\sum_i\rho_i\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Op}(a_i)\eta_i$. Homogeneity gives $\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta b_i(x,t\xi)=t^{r-|\beta|}\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\xi^\beta b_i(x,\xi)$; boundedness on compact $x$ sets times the unit sphere and the compact frequency annulus therefore proves $a_i\in S^r$. Step 1 makes $T_b$ an operator of order $r$. In any other chart its diagonal leading term is $\sum_i\rho_i\eta_i b=b$ by the coordinate-change formula. Differences of radial cutoffs, including after the linear cotangent change, have bounded frequency support on compact $x$ sets and hence belong to every symbol order by the defining estimates. Localizing with any $\chi,\psi$ and applying amplitude reduction thus gives $\chi T_b\psi-\chi\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Op}(\theta b)\psi\in\Psi^{r-1}$, as required.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, (3.4)–(3.5), Proposition 3.7; supplemental Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6), 3.12–3.15, read online. Agent-supplied details.

proof.text: For uniqueness, let $T_1,T_2$ have the same $b$ and put $H=T_1-T_2$. The definition of leading symbol gives $\rho_i H\eta_i\in\Psi^{r-1}$ in each common chart. Also $H=\sum_i\rho_i H\eta_i+\sum_i\rho_i H(1-\eta_i)$. In the second sum the output and input supports are separated. Expand the finite representations of $H$; their kernels are smooth off the diagonal by amplitude reduction, so after these separated cutoffs they are smooth kernels globally, extended by zero. Thus the second sum is smoothing, which belongs to every $\Psi^j$ by the empty-sum clause of the definition. This proves $H\in\Psi^{r-1}$ on all distributions. The same argument proves the local-to-global order test used below: for an operator with a finite local representation and smooth off-diagonal kernel, lower-order localized pieces $\rho_i H\eta_i$ imply the same lower global order.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, (3.4)–(3.5), Proposition 3.7; supplemental Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6), 3.12–3.15, read online. Agent-supplied details.

proof.text: For arbitrary $T\in\Psi^r$ and $S\in\Psi^s$, expand their finite chart representations. Terms involving a smooth kernel are smoothing by step 2. For a product of two chart terms, insert a finite partition in the intermediate variable subordinate to their overlap. Near the full diagonal $x=y=z$, refine further to coordinate neighborhoods trivializing all three bundles; compactness permits finitely many such neighborhoods. These pieces are compositions in one chart: after coordinate change, the Fourier-product theorem gives order $r+s$. The remaining pieces are smoothing. Indeed cover the compact set of triples by product neighborhoods, each either lying in one common chart or having the first two or last two coordinate neighborhoods with disjoint closures. A sufficiently fine finite refinement of the three spatial covers, with product partition weights, is subordinate to these neighborhoods. In a separated box the corresponding factor has a smooth localized kernel by step 1, and step 2 handles its composition. This argument applies to the compact supports of the chart terms and uses the same subordinate partitions and neighborhood cutoffs as step 3. Hence $ST\in\Psi^{r+s}$. The common-chart diagonal product of symbols is the matrix product, modulo order $r+s-1$, by the Fourier-product remainder estimate; finite sums and real parts preserve this conclusion.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, (3.4)–(3.5), Proposition 3.7; supplemental Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6), 3.12–3.15, read online. Agent-supplied details.

proof.text: Suppose now the leading symbols are $b,c$. Construct $T_b,S_c,T_{cb}$ as in step 3. Step 4 gives $T-T_b\in\Psi^{r-1}$ and $S-S_c\in\Psi^{s-1}$. Therefore $ST-S_cT_b=(S-S_c)T+S_c(T-T_b)$ has order $r+s-1$ by step 5. For the constructed operators, the common-chart leading product in step 5 is $cb$: the diagonal partition weights sum to $1\cdot1$, and the intermediate frame changes cancel. More explicitly, the outer chart weights give $(\sum_j\rho_j\eta_j)c(\sum_i\rho_i\eta_i)b=cb$. The Fourier-product and coordinate-change remainders are of order $r+s-1$. Consequently each localization of $S_cT_b-T_{cb}$ has that order; its off-diagonal kernel is smooth by the product argument of step 5. Step 4's local-to-global test gives $S_cT_b-T_{cb}\in\Psi^{r+s-1}$. Localizing the resulting equality proves that $ST$ has leading symbol $cb$. Its homogeneity degree is $r+s$ and its conjugation symmetry follows from $\overline{cb}=\bar c\bar b$.

proof.text: Finally Fourier inversion on Schwartz functions, after the frequency substitution $\xi=2\pi\zeta$, gives $\operatorname{Op}(1)=\mathrm{id}$ and $\operatorname{Op}(\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}a_\alpha(x)(i\xi)^\alpha)=\sum a_\alpha\partial^\alpha$ on chart tests. These are also identities of the bilinear transposes, by integration by parts with both spatial cutoffs; hence they are identities on all distributions under the conventions of the definition. The polynomial symbol belongs to $S^k$. Its terms of degree less than $k$ have order at most $k-1$; the difference between its top term and $\theta p_k$ has compact frequency support and hence all orders. A finite partition gives $D=\sum_i\rho_iD\eta_i$ exactly, since $\eta_i=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i$ and $D$ is differential. This proves global order $k$. The chain and Leibniz rules give the transition formula directly: terms in which any derivative hits a frame coefficient or a previously differentiated coordinate coefficient have at most $k-1$ derivatives on the input section. The remaining terms are the product of $k$ first coordinate derivatives, with the output and inverse input frame factors; replacing each derivative by $i\xi$ gives exactly the cotangent pullback and these frame factors. Thus $p_k$ is a global bundle symbol and the preceding local remainder calculation proves precisely the prescribed leading-symbol condition. Its real symmetry is $(i(-\xi))^\alpha=\overline{(i\xi)^\alpha}$. For $k=0$ the same compact-frequency argument applies; for the identity it yields order zero and leading symbol $\mathrm{id}$.
